articles.title: Delhi shocker: 2 minors among 3 held after teenager stabbed ‘16 times’
articles.summary: Delhi Anand Parbat teen stabbed to death after lane argument; police arrest 19-year-old and apprehend two minors within 7 hours, recover knife.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Police have apprehended a youth and two minors who allegedly murdered a 17-year-old boy, stabbing him multiple times in central Delhi’s Anand Parbat, after they brushed past each other in a narrow lane Tuesday.The murdered boy’s brother said he was stabbed 16 times. Police said seven to eight stab wounds have been found on the teenager’s body. “My mother is in denial,” said 18-year-old Mayank Dhingra, the boy’s brother. "She keeps asking me, ‘where is my son? I hope he got a good bandage. When will he be discharged?’ How do I keep telling her he is no more?” he asked.The teenager, a resident of Anand Parbat, was found injured in Gali No. 16, Than Singh Road, Tuesday night. A constable and some people who were nearby rushed him to Jeevan Mala Hospital, where doctors declared him brought dead. Police got a call around 8.30pm.The boy’s cousin Hrithik said the family was informed while the teenager was in hospital. “The doctor told us he had been stabbed multiple times. We were shocked. How could someone do this? He was just a teenager,” he said.An FIR under Section 103(1) of BNS, which provides for punishment for murder, was registered at Anand Parbat police station Tuesday. DCP (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said CCTV footage, technical surveillance and local information helped the cops identify the attackers.Tushar (19), of Anand Parbat, was arrested, while two juveniles, aged 17 and 15, were apprehended from the area within seven hours of the murder. Police also found the knife they had allegedly used on the boy. Investigators have also not found any history of enmity between the boy and the trio.The three attackers told police that they were walking through Gali No. 16 and the boy was coming from the opposite direction. They accidentally collided while passing each other, following which an argument broke out. Police said the altercation escalated and they allegedly stabbed the teenager and fled.At the mortuary, as Mayank waited for his brother’s body, he recounted the moments before and after the family came to know about the murder. He said he was returning home Tuesday evening, while his mother was in a nearby lane at his aunt’s house.When she was first told about the attack, the boy’s mum “ran from one place to another.” Mayank said: “She finally found out that my brother was at a hospital. We rushed there. He had been stabbed 16 times. My brother had no enmity with anyone.”Mayank said his brother had stepped out of the house after their grandmother asked him to bring her some household goods. articles.title: Médico expõe prontuário e faz piada com paciente; HC vê preconceito  | G1
articles.standfirst: Publicação no X mostrou peso, altura, IMC e doença respiratória; hospital informou que tomaria providências, mas não esclareceu se o profissional foi afastado.
articles.summary: Publicação no X mostrou peso, altura, IMC e doença respiratória; hospital informou que tomaria providências, mas não esclareceu se o profissional foi afastado.
articles.body:
Médico expõe prontuário e faz piada com paciente; HC vê preconceito — Foto: reprodução X

Um médico residente do Hospital das Clínicas da Faculdade de Medicina de Ribeirão Preto da Universidade de São Paulo (HCFMRP-USP) publicou nas redes sociais uma imagem de um prontuário médico com tom de piada sobre um paciente com sobrepeso atendido na instituição. (Veja a imagem acima)

A postagem, feita no dia 21 de setembro, mostra uma imagem da tela com os dados do paciente. Na publicação, ele "desabafa" que esse é o tipo de situação que se enfrenta no hospital, e sinaliza o peso, IMC e altura do paciente.

O post teve ao menos 100 mil visualizações antes de ser apagado pelo profissional, depois que outros profissionais alertaram que a situação, além de expor o paciente a uma posição vexatória, também expunha dados sensíveis -- o que pode ser classificado como infração ética.

O g1 procurou o HCFMRP-USP sobre o caso. O hospital confirmou que o médico faz parte do quadro de residentes e classificou a atitude como preconceituosa.

“O HCFMRP-USP tomou ciência da publicação em rede social e considera a atitude preconceituosa. Embora não tenha ocorrido exposição de identidade, a publicação é inadequada e não condiz com a postura profissional preconizada por esta instituição. Já estamos tomando providências para que a postagem seja removida e que a conduta não se repita”, informou o hospital.

O g1 questionou se o médico segue atendendo na unidade ou recebeu alguma punição pela exposição, mas não obteve retorno até a publicação.

O g1 também procurou o Conselho Federal de Medicina (CFM) sobre o caso, mas não teve retorno até a publicação.

Exposição é infração ética e fere a LGPD

Advogados ouvidos pelo g1 avaliam que o médico, ao expor o prontuário, comete infração ética e fere a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados.

O advogado especialista em bioética, Henderson Furst, explica que o Código de Ética Médica impede o compartilhamento das informações, ainda mais no tom vexatório, como foi feito na publicação.

O especialista explica que, ainda que não seja identificável ao público geral, já que não tem nome, o paciente e seus familiares podem se identificar.

"O caso expõe um fenômeno preocupante, que é a perda de sensibilidade ética de jovens profissionais da saúde. Há várias esferas de ilicitude. A mais evidente dela é a ética, pois fere diverso dispositivos do Código de Ética Médica. Mas potencialmente há crime, improbidade administrativa e ilícito civil também.

Muito embora as condições de exercício da medicina e outras profissões da saúde no Brasil sejam as mais adversas, extenuantes e exaustivas, não se pode esquecer que são pessoas hipervulneráveis que depositam sua confiança e esperança como única solução no sistema de saúde", explica.

articles.title: Mulher é detida por suspeita de tentativa de estupro em Arraial | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a vítima, suspeita apresentava comportamento obsessivo e a ameaçou com uma faca e uma tesoura dentro da residência.
articles.summary: Segundo a vítima, suspeita apresentava comportamento obsessivo e a ameaçou com uma faca e uma tesoura dentro da residência.
articles.body:
A vítima afirmou que a suspeita vinha demonstrando comportamento obsessivo e intimidador. — Foto: Prefeitura de Arraial do Cabo

Uma mulher foi detida nesta quarta-feira (23), em Arraial do Cabo , na Região dos Lagos do Rio, sob suspeita de perseguir e tentar estuprar outra mulher.

Segundo o depoimento da vítima, a suspeita iniciou uma discussão e, em seguida, invadiu a residência, onde teria ocorrido a tentativa de estupro. Ainda de acordo com o relato, a mulher utilizou uma faca e uma tesoura para ameaçá-la.

A ocorrência foi atendida pela Guarda Civil Municipal de Arraial do Cabo, por meio da Patrulha Maria da Penha e da Ronda Ostensiva Municipal (Romu).

A vítima afirmou que a suspeita vinha demonstrando comportamento obsessivo e intimidador.

O caso chegou ao conhecimento das forças de segurança após as duas mulheres procurarem atendimento no Hospital Geral de Arraial do Cabo. Seguindo o protocolo de proteção à mulher adotado pela unidade de saúde, a equipe médica acionou a Patrulha Maria da Penha para prestar acolhimento à vítima.

A Romu prestou apoio à ocorrência e conduziu a suspeita para a Delegacia Especializada de Atendimento à Mulher (Deam), onde ela permaneceu detida à disposição da Justiça.

O caso segue sob investigação das autoridades competentes.

articles.title: Morte de Leopoldo Barros Teixeira: Copiloto de Rick é velado em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Leopoldo Barros Teixeira, de 34 anos, estava em aeronave que caiu a caminho da Serra Catarinense com cinco ocupantes. Corpo será sepultado nesta quinta-feira (24).
articles.summary: Leopoldo Barros Teixeira morreu na queda de helicóptero com o cantor Rick em Santa Catarina; o corpo do copiloto será sepultado nesta quinta em Pongaí.
articles.body:
A morte de Leopoldo Barros Teixeira, de 34 anos, comoveu a população de Pongaí (SP), cidade de pouco mais de 3 mil moradores onde ele cresceu. A prefeitura decretou luto oficial de três dias, e familiares e amigos se reuniram na Igreja Matriz da cidade para a última despedida.

Leopoldo ocupava o assento de copiloto no helicóptero que caiu em Santa Catarina enquanto transportava o cantor Rick, da dupla Rick & Renner. A aeronave desapareceu na tarde de segunda-feira (21) após decolar de Porto Belo com destino a São Joaquim .

Copiloto que morreu em queda de helicóptero com Rick é velado na Igreja Matriz de Pongaí — Foto: Andressa Lara/TV TEM/Reprodução

O corpo de Leopoldo é velado na Paróquia São José desde as 20h desta quarta-feira (23) . O sepultamento está marcado para a manhã desta quinta-feira (24), a partir das 10h, no Cemitério Municipal.

Os destroços e os corpos dos cinco ocupantes da aeronave foram localizados na terça-feira (22) , em uma área de mata fechada e montanhosa, após uma intensa operação de resgate.

O impacto da tragédia foi imediato entre os moradores de Pongaí, onde a família do piloto era muito conhecida.

"Essa notícia acabou pegando a cidade de surpresa e deixou todo mundo muito triste, em luto. Foi, infelizmente, como uma bomba que caiu para todos nós. O Leopoldo era um menino fantástico, do bem. Sonhava desde sempre em voar, em ser piloto, e infelizmente acabou acontecendo essa tragédia com uma coisa que ele tanto sonhou na vida", relatou o empresário Adilson Brumatti, amigo da família, em entrevista à TV TEM .

O sentimento de consternação também é compartilhado pelo professor Heli Aroni, que acompanhou o crescimento do piloto desde os tempos de escola.

"A gente conversou há pouco tempo porque ele estava muito contente com o trabalho. Por ser uma cidade pequena, todo mundo se conhece. Ele era um menino muito amoroso com todos. O sonho dele era ser piloto de helicóptero, ele batalhou e conseguiu. Essa notícia abalou a nossa pequena Pongaí", disse o professor.

Os corpos foram liberados do Instituto Médico Legal (IML) de Florianópolis (SC) na madrugada desta quarta-feira, por volta da 1h30, após reconhecimento por exame papiloscópico. Segundo a família, o corpo de Leopoldo foi encaminhado para uma funerária em Osasco (SP) antes de seguir para Pongaí.

Paróquia São José, Igreja Matriz em Pongaí recebe o velório do copiloto Leopoldo Barros Teixeira — Foto: Andressa Lara/TV TEM

O piloto havia retomado a carreira na aviação civil no ano passado . Segundo o irmão dele, Lincoln Barros Teixeira, ao trabalhar com aviação ele realizava um sonho de juventude.

"Nós falamos para ele seguir o sonho dele. Sempre o incentivamos. Ele morreu, mas morreu feliz fazendo o que amava", disse o irmão.

Leopoldo Barros Teixeira atuava como copiloto no helicóptero que caiu com o cantor Rick, da dupla Rick e Renner — Foto: Reprodução

Lincoln explicou que ele e o irmão nasceram em Pirajuí (SP), já que Pongaí (SP), cidade onde cresceram, não possui maternidade. Ainda segundo o irmão, Leopoldo não tinha filhos, era solteiro e morava em Itapema, no Litoral Norte de Santa Catarina, onde trabalhava com helicópteros.

Lincoln ainda relatou que a família tentou entrar em contato com Leopoldo na segunda-feira (21), mas não conseguiu. A falta de notícias deu início a uma espera angustiante até a confirmação da morte.

“A gente tentou entrar em contato com ele e não conseguimos. Aí foi toda essa agonia”, disse.

Leopoldo Barros Teixeira era natural de Pongaí (SP) — Foto: Reprodução

O irmão também relembrou que a paixão de Leopoldo por helicópteros surgiu na juventude, graças ao convívio com amigos da família. Após um primeiro voo, ele decidiu fazer o curso e, depois de um período parado, resolveu retomar o sonho com o apoio da família.

Lincoln ainda compartilhou que o irmão era muito querido por todos: "ele é muito querido, estamos recebendo muitas mensagens, muita gente querendo vir no velório".

Coroas de flores lotam a Igreja Matriz de Pongaí no velório de Leopoldo Barros Teixeira — Foto: TV TEM/Reprodução

Infográfico mostra local aproximado das buscas por helicóptero desaparecido em SC — Foto: Arte/g1

Os bombeiros receberam uma chamada sobre o desaparecimento por volta das 16h. A operação passou a se concentrar em dois pontos: uma área inicialmente indicada como possível local da queda e a região onde foi registrado o último sinal de celular de um dos ocupantes.

A região onde os destroços foram encontrados tem áreas que variam entre montanha, planície e mata fechada.

A operação de buscas contou com uma aeronave (que encontrou os destroços), aproximadamente 40 bombeiros, dois cães farejadores, mais de 10 viaturas e drones com capacidade de identificação térmica.

articles.title: SFX abre 40 vagas para estágio na área da saúde no Vale do Aço | G1
articles.standfirst: Inscrições podem ser feitas até 2 de outubro. Programa oferece bolsa de R$ 300 e oportunidades para estudantes de diferentes áreas da saúde.
articles.summary: Estudantes de graduação podem se inscrever até 2 de outubro. Programa oferece bolsa de R$ 300 e vagas em diferentes áreas da saúde.
articles.body:
Hospital Márcio Cunha em Ipatinga — Foto: Divulgação

A Fundação São Francisco Xavier (FSFX) abriu 40 vagas para o Programa Estágio de Férias 2027, destinado a estudantes de graduação. As inscrições seguem até 2 de outubro e devem ser feitas pelo site da instituição.

As oportunidades são para diferentes áreas da saúde em unidades da FSFX no Vale do Aço. O estágio começa em 4 de janeiro, com treinamento presencial em Ipatinga , e termina no dia 31. No dia 5, haverá treinamento on-line, e as atividades nas unidades começam em 6 de janeiro.

Segundo o edital, os selecionados receberão bolsa-auxílio de R$ 300, vale-transporte e seguro contra acidentes pessoais. A alimentação será oferecida aos estagiários que atuarem em unidades que possuem refeitório próprio.

As vagas têm carga horária de seis horas por dia, 30 horas semanais e 120 horas no total. Os horários variam conforme a área escolhida.

Para concorrer, o estudante precisa estar matriculado em uma instituição de ensino brasileira conveniada à FSFX e cursar, no mínimo, o período exigido para a oportunidade escolhida. A relação das instituições conveniadas está disponível no edital.

Cada candidato pode se inscrever em apenas uma modalidade de estágio . Caso faça mais de uma inscrição, somente a primeira cadastrada será considerada.

As oportunidades estão distribuídas entre as seguintes áreas:

Medicina (Oncologia Clínica/Radioterapia)

As atividades serão desenvolvidas no Hospital Márcio Cunha I e II, na Unidade de Oncologia e em unidades do Usifamília em Ipatinga e Coronel Fabriciano, conforme a vaga escolhida.

De acordo com o edital, o estágio é extracurricular, na modalidade não obrigatória . Os participantes poderão observar e auxiliar nas atividades, mas não poderão realizar procedimentos assistenciais sem a supervisão do profissional responsável.

Para a coordenadora de Ensino e Pesquisa da FSFX, Alessandra Borges, a experiência também contribui para a formação dos estudantes.

“Durante esse período, os estudantes têm contato com equipes altamente qualificadas, acompanham processos assistenciais e desenvolvem uma visão ampliada sobre o cuidado ao paciente. [...] Além do aprendizado técnico, a experiência contribui para o crescimento profissional e para a construção de uma carreira mais sólida e alinhada às necessidades do mercado”.

A seleção será feita por meio de uma prova técnica on-line, marcada para 24 de outubro . Serão 15 questões, divididas entre conhecimentos gerais para profissionais da saúde, conhecimentos sobre a FSFX e conteúdos relacionados à área escolhida pelo candidato.

A avaliação valerá 100 pontos, e serão classificados os candidatos que alcançarem pelo menos 60. A classificação seguirá a pontuação em ordem decrescente e o número de vagas disponível em cada área.

O resultado está previsto para 27 de outubro , e a convocação será feita no dia seguinte. O edital também prevê segunda chamada em 3 de novembro, em caso de desistência ou desclassificação durante as etapas admissionais.

As inscrições seguem até as 23h59 de 2 de outubro. No formulário, o estudante deve preencher os dados pessoais e da instituição de ensino e indicar a modalidade de estágio escolhida.

articles.title: Professora de pilates que morreu era considerada 'atleta da família' | G1
articles.standfirst: Lorraynne Bueno era educadora física há 10 anos. Ela morreu durante uma internação no Hospital Regional de Gurupi (HRG), no sul do Tocantins.
articles.summary: Lorraynne Bueno era educadora física há 10 anos. Ela morreu durante uma internação no Hospital Regional de Gurupi (HRG), no sul do Tocantins.
articles.body:
A morte da professora de pilates Lorraynne Bueno de Araújo, de 32 anos, comoveu familiares e amigos. Educadora física com dez anos de experiência, ela era condiderada a "atleta da família", segundo conta a irmã Dayane Ribeiro Dias.

"Ela sempre foi uma menina super saudável, a atleta da família e uma das profissionais mais bem conceituadas de Gurupi . Uma pessoa maravilhosa, sempre prestativa com os outros, um amor", comentou.

Lorraynne morreu durante internação no Hospital Regional de Gurupi (HRG) , no sul do Tocantins. Ela faria um teste para confirmar a suspeita de Covid-19, mas morreu na noite de segunda-feira (21) antes que o exame fosse realizado.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

Lorraynne Bueno era instrutora de pilates há 10 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

Dedicada a promover o bem-estar físico, a professora publicou artigo científico sobre os benefícios do pilates para a imagem corporal de mulheres adultas e também usava as redes sociais para dar dicas de consciência corporal.

Lorraynne havia se casado há dez meses e não tinha filhos. Lembrada como uma pessoa de bom humor, a irmã afirma que ela gostava de dançar forró nos tempos livres.

"Ela gostava de dançar, era muito extrovertida, amava comer bem e gostava de comida japonesa. Minha irmã era super saudável, a mais sadia da família", comentou Dayane.

articles.title: Engavetamento na Rodovia Santos Dumont em Campinas deixa feridos | G1
articles.standfirst: Colisão ocorreu na manhã desta quinta-feira (24) e chegou a interditar uma das faixas da via. Duas pessoas precisaram de atendimento médico.
articles.summary: Engavetamento na Rodovia Santos Dumont envolveu quatro carros e deixou duas pessoas feridas em Campinas na manhã desta quinta-feira (24).
articles.body:
Engavetamento entre quatro carros deixa feridos na Rodovia Santos Dumont, em Campinas — Foto: Sueli Santos

Um engavetamento envolvendo quatro veículos de passeio deixou duas pessoas feridas na Rodovia Santos Dumont (SP-075), em Campinas (SP), na manhã desta quinta-feira (24).

O acidente aconteceu na altura do quilômetro 76, na pista sentido Campinas, por volta das 9h08.

De acordo com a concessionária Via Colinas, responsável pela administração do trecho, duas pessoas saíram ilesas e duas precisaram de atendimento :

Uma vítima com ferimentos leves foi levada à UPA São José;

Uma vítima com ferimentos moderados foi encaminhada ao Hospital Renascença.

A colisão ocorreu pela faixa 2 da rodovia, que precisou ficar interditada durante o atendimento da ocorrência.

Segundo a concessionária, a pista foi totalmente liberada às 9h47, quando todos os carros foram retirados da faixa de rolamento .

Os veículos foram levados para o acostamento e aguardam a remoção para fora da rodovia.

articles.title: NHS staff investigated over access to dead teenager's medical records
articles.summary: Oliver McGowan, who died in 2016, may have had his medical records accessed inappropriately after his death by NHS staff in Bristol.
articles.body:
The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed inappropriately for years after his death.

Paula McGowan, whose 18-year-old autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Bristol Foundation NHS Trust may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year.

Three nursing staff are under formal investigation, while a doctor who no longer works for the trust has self-referred to the General Medical Council. Another member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.

The trust said it was "deeply sorry" for any stress and anxiety caused.

It said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

It is the latest case involving concerns that NHS staff may have accessed patient records without a legitimate professional reason. In July the head of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, issued a "stark warning" that staff could face the sack or even prison for doing so.

This month an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years.

Oliver, who had a mild learning disability and epilepsy, died in 2016 at Southmead Hospital in Bristol after being given anti-psychotic medication that his family had repeatedly warned he should not receive.

After requesting information about his medical records, his mother was told that 38 people had accessed the data since his death, with 637 items viewed and 67 printed off.

Most access was appropriate and linked to complaints, legal proceedings, and the coroner's inquest into his death.

But three nursing staff not involved in his care are currently under formal investigation after initial inquiries could find no evidence they had a legitimate reason to view her son's records.

A fourth member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.

McGowan said she was told that one nurse wanted to view the files as they had a general interest in anti-psychotic drugs and the care of patients with a learning disability.

The trust is also looking into 13 other cases involving former staff, including doctors, nurses and clerical workers, to establish if that access was appropriate or not.

One doctor, who no longer works at the trust, has already referred themselves to the medical regulator, the GMC, after being approached by the hospital.

Autistic teen's hospital death was 'avoidable'

McGowan told the BBC she was "deeply hurt, deeply disappointed" after being told about the investigation, which is ongoing.

"I've always been open and honest but there are deeply personal things in Oliver's [medical] notes that I don't tell anybody," she said.

"He died in pain and it's not pleasant if that side of Oliver's death has been accessed."

Her husband, Tom McGowan, said that the risk of unauthorised access to medical records had increased as more information is stored on digital, cloud-based platforms.

"It's a weakness in the system and action needs to be taken now to tighten up controls," he said.

Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete".

"Every patient and family has the right to expect that their personal information will be treated with care, respect and confidentiality," said Prof Steve Hams, the trust's chief nursing and improvement officer.

"Any concern that records may have been accessed without a legitimate reason is something we take extremely seriously."

The trust said that, should any staff misconduct be identified, "appropriate action will be taken through the relevant processes".

NHS medical records can contain highly sensitive personal information, ranging from test results and hospital discharge summaries to details of prescriptions and medications.

That extends well beyond the information available to patients through the NHS app and may include safeguarding concerns, risk assessments, correspondence between healthcare professionals and detailed consultation notes.

There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access.

Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information.

Doctors, nurses and other healthcare staff often need fast access, particularly in emergencies.

However, they should only view confidential information when they have a legitimate work-related reason and the right authorisation.

IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when.

NHS England said any instance of staff looking at records without a valid reason would be "wholly unacceptable, a disgraceful breach of patients' trust and against the law".

"We have been crystal clear that staff could face disciplinary action for any breaches, including the loss of their job and potential criminal prosecution," added a spokesman.

articles.title: Parents accuse Oregon hospital of making them drive dead baby home to Seattle: lawsuit
articles.summary: A Seattle couple's $10 million lawsuit alleges Salem Health staff pressured them to transport their deceased baby's body home in their personal vehicle.
articles.body: A Seattle couple is suing after hospital staff in Oregon told them to drive the body of their nearly 9-month-old son four hours home in their private car following his sudden death in an emergency room. Aleksandr and Nataliya Yeremeyev filed a $10 million lawsuit against Salem Health and Dr. Stefani Sorensen. The parents had allegedly sought respectful and dignified care and transportation of the remains of their son, Michael, but the lawsuit alleges staff insisted they bring the body back home with them. Michael was born with Down syndrome and spent the first six months of his life at Seattle Children's Hospital. "His parents had made sure that he had received really excellent care. So, I think it was a really, really sad and just very tragic way for his life to end and for it to be so undignified right there at the end," Anna Bruckenhoefer, the family's attorney, said in a statement, according to Fox 13. TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH On September 22, 2024, the family was visiting Salem, Oregon, for a religious retreat when Michael developed rapid, shallow breathing late at night and was rushed to the emergency room at Salem Health Hospital, where he died, according to the complaint. When the parents asked how to arrange respectful transport to send Michael’s body back home to Seattle, hospital staff allegedly pushed back on the suggestion to contact a local funeral home because it would be "too expensive" and instead pressured the family to bring their son’s body with them in their own car, which they ended up doing due to feeling like they had no other option. "They have repeatedly asked the hospital for assistance in helping them with what are the next steps," Bruckenhoefer said. "This was all occurring overnight. They felt rushed that they had to make quick decisions and the hospital left them with no choice other than to take Michael's body with them and head back to Seattle." Aleksandr drove about four hours from Salem to Seattle with his son’s body laid across the backseat, while his wife and other children followed in a separate car. FAMILY OF TODDLER FOUND ALIVE IN MORGUE AFTER BEING DECLARED DEAD PLANS LEGAL ACTION He suffered severe emotional distress as he feared police stops, car crashes and the visible deterioration of his child's body, according to the lawsuit. When he arrived at a Seattle funeral home, the father had to clean bodily fluids that leaked onto the seat during the trip. "It is legal in the state of Oregon and in the state of Washington to transport a deceased with the proper permits. But that is not what our clients wanted to do here. They were looking for help. They were looking for guidance. They were looking for the hospital to tell them, "These are the next steps,'" Bruckenhoefer said. "This is a hospital. It's an emergency department. Unfortunately, death is something that they are accustomed to and that they deal with. They should have had procedures and protocols in place to assist the Yeremeyev’s while they were dealing with literally the worst moment of their lives. Instead, what they did is they just compounded their grief by essentially telling them that they were on their own in this." "No parents, no loved ones should ever be placed in the position that the Yeremeyev’s were placed in," Bruckenhoefer added. "Just completely surprised that something like this would happen in 2026." The lawsuit names Salem Health Hospitals & Clinics, Salem Health, Salem Emergency Physicians Service and Sorensen as defendants, alleging direct negligence, vicarious liability, and a breach of the heightened duty of care owed to bereaved parents for the respectful treatment and custody of a child's body. The family is seeking $10 million in non-economic damages for severe emotional distress and psychological trauma, although they plan to amend the complaint to include punitive damages. Salem Health Hospital said out of respect for privacy and because the matter is in litigation, it is unable to discuss the details of the child's care. "Salem Hospital responded in accordance with the family’s wishes and followed both hospital policy and Oregon state law in consultation with the appropriate local authorities, including the medical examiner," Salem Health told Fox 13 in a statement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Care with respect is a guiding principle of clinical practice at Salem Hospital and remains central to how we support patients and families during some of life's most difficult moments. We recognize the profound grief families experience following the loss of a loved one and treat every patient and family with empathy, dignity, and respect," the statement continued.

articles.title: Trump’s FDA pick to face scrutiny over abortion pill access at confirmation hearing
articles.summary: Dr. Heidi Overton is also expected to address President Donald Trump’s claim labeling the measles vaccine “lethal.”
articles.body: Dr. Heidi Overton, a fierce opponent of abortion rights, is set to appear before senators Thursday for her confirmation hearing to lead the Food and Drug Administration. The hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee comes as the FDA faces pressure from Republicans, including the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., to tighten access to the abortion pill mifepristone. Cassidy, who is a key vote in Overton’s confirmation, has been pushing the administration to reverse a Biden-era rule that allows mifepristone to be prescribed via telemedicine and sent through the mail. In a committee report published last month, Cassidy accused the makers of mifepristone of failing to meet their legal responsibilities to ensure compliance with FDA safety regulations, particularly when the pills are sold online through third-party providers. At a hearing in January, Cassidy called on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the previous FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary, to complete a safety review that they both promised during their confirmation hearings. In June, the FDA said it launched a new safety study on mifepristone. Art Caplan, the head of the medical ethics division at NYU Grossman School of Medicine in New York City, said Overton’s views on abortion appear to align with Cassidy’s. Overton, a preventive medicine physician, currently serves as a domestic policy official in the White House. Prior to that, she worked as chief policy officer at the conservative think tank America First Policy Institute, where she praised the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade and called for strict restrictions on medication abortion, claiming that it is “dangerous to women.” (Studies have shown that the drug, even when taken at home, is safe and effective.) If confirmed, Overton would take over an agency that has been without a permanent commissioner since Makary resigned in May, in part over the administration’s decision to authorize several fruit-flavored vapes for adults. As commissioner, Overton would serve as a key ally to Kennedy, whose department oversees the FDA. Overton is a proponent of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. She also appeared alongside President Donald Trump in August when he announced an executive order aimed at reducing the number of vaccines routinely recommended for children. Trump nominated her to lead the agency days later. Senators are likely to grill her about her own views on vaccines, according to Dorit Reiss, a professor of law and vaccine policy expert at the University of California Law San Francisco. On CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Cassidy — who has also aggressively questioned and pressed several Trump administration nominees on vaccines — said Overton must acknowledge that Trump’s claim that the measles vaccine is lethal is “absurd” when she appears before his committee. Trump made the comment during the August signing of his vaccine executive order. “I think she made it clear she’s a supporter of Kennedy’s vaccine agenda, at least,” Reiss said. “Dr. Overton seems like another example of an appointee who is, primarily, appointed for political opinions, without an emphasis on qualifications.” Overton, Reiss said, doesn’t appear to have expertise in clinical trials, managing an agency or any of the products the FDA regulates. “It’s reasonable for an administration to want someone sympathetic to their views,” Reiss said, “but FDA commissioner is a hard job that requires the ability to manage a large and complex agency that does important work.” “As an MD/PhD who helped President Trump deliver on Operation Warp Speed during his first term, Dr. Heidi Overton will ensure that policymaking is guided solely by Gold Standard Science at the FDA,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement. Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting FDA commissioner, said food safety will be another major issue waiting for her at the FDA. The agency has spent much of the summer responding to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks and recalls, including a massive cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce that sickened more than 12,000 people across multiple states. The outbreak has also raised questions about how quickly the FDA can trace contaminated food back to its source and whether the agency has enough staff to respond to outbreaks after thousands of employees left or were laid off over the past year. “After the experience of the past 18 months, it’s very important to restore public and industry confidence that decisions being made by FDA, including those by leadership, are science-based, transparent and consistent,” Ostroff said.

images.caption: Dr. Heidi Overton, deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, in the Oval Office of the White House on Aug. 31, 2026.

articles.title: People are ditching their vapes only to pick up another surprising habit
articles.summary: E-cigarettes promised a clean off-ramp from smoking, but severe vape withdrawal is pushing former smokers back to traditional cigarettes, experts warn.
articles.body: E-cigarettes have long been used as an alternative to traditional smoking, but public health data suggests some adults trying to quit vaping are turning back to cigarettes. Recent data from Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) shows that some smokers and dual users who stop vaping opt for traditional tobacco products instead, a shift that addiction specialists say may be driven by nicotine dependence and the challenges of withdrawal. Trent Carter, a board-certified nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health — a behavioral and mental health practice based in New Mexico — said that while the shift from vapes back to cigarettes might seem counterintuitive, there are behavioral reasons some users make the switch. SINGLE WORKOUT CUTS CRAVINGS, OFFERING NEW HOPE FOR SMOKERS TRYING TO QUIT "Vaping can become constant throughout the day, whereas a cigarette is more of a defined episode," Carter told Fox News Digital. "Subconsciously, you may not even realize that you’re constantly vaping throughout the day, whereas cigarettes you feel like you're more in control because you have to think about it. You [have] to go outside, you [have] to light it up." Unlike cigarettes, vaping can be done throughout the day and often indoors. That easy access can lead to more nicotine use and reinforce the hand-to-mouth habit, according to the expert. High potency, severe withdrawal E-cigarettes can be highly addictive because of the way they deliver nicotine. Many vaping devices use highly concentrated nicotine salts, allowing users to inhale large doses with each puff compared to traditional cigarettes. "If you're consuming a large amount with every single puff ... it's going to be harder to stop when compared to a lower dose," Carter said. SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA Nicotine dependence alters brain chemistry by stimulating neurotransmitters like dopamine that govern mood and pleasure, according to Cleveland Clinic. When someone abruptly cuts off high-volume intake, it can trigger rapid withdrawal symptoms, ranging from intense cravings and irritability to severe sleep disturbances and brain fog. Because high-potency vapes drive up physical tolerance, standard quitting aids — like over-the-counter patches or nicotine gum — can sometimes feel inadequate to a user seeking immediate relief. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "While a patch or gum could definitely help with the nicotine cravings, if you're not addressing the behavioral aspect of it, then you're really falling short," Carter said. "You're leaving a huge component of why they may be smoking — whether it's because of anxiety or even insomnia during the day." False sense of security When e-cigarettes first hit the market, early public messaging framed them as a healthier, doctor-approved alternative to smoking, which gave many consumers a false sense of security about how difficult it would be to drop the habit, according to Carter. "If you're being told something is safe or doctor-approved, we tend to feel we're making the right choice," Carter said. "While traditional cigarettes have toxins that e-cigarettes do not, if your daily consumption of nicotine becomes much higher, we find ourselves in a nasty cycle. You got rid of the toxins, but now you're consuming much more nicotine." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The elevated chemical intake carries a physical and mental toll, Carter cautioned. Heavy, uninterrupted nicotine ingestion can trigger blood pressure spikes, elevated heart rates, sleep disruption and heightened anxiety. Breaking the dependency loop For people trying to quit vaping, health providers warn that switching to cigarettes reintroduces harmful toxins, tar and carbon monoxide. Instead of switching between vaping and cigarettes, addiction specialists recommend medically supervised strategies that combine behavioral therapy with gradual nicotine reduction. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine," Carter said. "The goal should be to treat the dependence itself." "It's not trading one for the other, but finding the underlying cause and addressing that head-on — that's how someone truly takes steps in the right direction." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For those struggling to exit the cycle, Carter advises building self-awareness and immediately consulting a licensed addiction or mental health professional who can recommend a personalized recovery plan.

articles.title: Walking This Many Steps Extra Each Day Could Reduce Heart Disease Risk
articles.summary: It’s not necessary to walk 10,000 steps a day to reduce heart disease risk, study finds. Add 1,000 steps to your existing routine to see heart health benefits.
articles.body: Walking 10,000 steps a day is a trendy goal, but you don’t need that many steps to help prevent heart disease. The benefits for a healthier heart start showing up much earlier, especially if you extend your walking routine by just a few minutes. A recent study looked at the walking habits of thousands of people with high blood pressure and found small changes can make a big difference. Heart Health Tip of the Day: Walk an Extra 1,000 Steps a Day Every additional 1,000 steps walked per day — up to 10,000 steps — was associated with a significantly lower risk of death, heart failure and heart attacks, the study published in August in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology found. It works whether you now walk 2,000 or 5,000 steps a day. Every 1,000-step increase in the daily step count lowered the risk by about 17%, particularly when people walked faster, the paper noted. Daily step counts “well below” 10,000 steps a day were still associated with lower risk of major heart problems, the authors wrote. The risk reductions continued up to at least 7,000 steps a day, an accompanying editorial, titled “Every step counts and more steps count more,” pointed out. “The bottom line — what we need to highlight is: Don’t be sedentary. Try to be more active,” Dr. Annapoorna Kini, a cardiologist at the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, tells TODAY.com. She was not involved in the study. “The number of 10,000 (steps) can come out. … Whatever you could do, try to add a little bit more, and that will be beneficial.” Why It Matters Adults should get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week, the type of exercise that makes people breathe harder, have a higher heart rate and perspire, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes. Fast walking is one example of activities that require moderate effort. “Walking is easy, can be done any time, and it is free,” Kini says. “Most people who don’t exercise (can) at least start somewhere.” When the doctor sees sedentary patients with high blood pressure and high cholesterol, she recommends lifestyle changes such as a healthier diet and more exercise. But “most people do not follow lifestyle modification because it’s very hard thing to do,” Kini says. “Then we say, ‘You know what? Start walking.’” Walking can be done outdoors or indoors. The steps are easily measured by a phone or smartwatch, and they can add up throughout the day, though one long walk has a bigger payoff for the heart than several shorter ones, research has found. How to Get Started Add an extra 1,000 steps to your routine — it doesn’t take a lot of time or energy. It’s the equivalent of 10 minutes of brisk walking or two laps around a standard outdoor running track. If you’re in a city, it’s the equivalent of walking about five city blocks. Kini just tells her patients to do as much as they can. You don’t have to get to 10,000 steps — that target has long been promoted without a scientific foundation, the editorial notes. About 7,000 steps a day seems to be the “optimal dose,” the authors of the new study add. Download the Start TODAY app for walking challenges, meal plans and workouts designed for every fitness level. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Is It Healthy to Eat Avocado Every Day? This Is the No. 1 Thing to Keep in Mind, Dietitian Says
articles.summary: Avocado is a uniquely healthy food that’s used in a huge variety of recipes. And while you can eat it every day, you should keep this in mind, dietitian says.
articles.body: With it’s creamy texture and vibrant green flesh, avocado is a unique — and uniquely healthy — food that’s used in a variety of culinary contexts. But is avocado good enough for you to eat every day? It certainly can be, says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. Not only does avocado provide a big dose of heart-healthy fats, it’s also full of other nutrients that support your overall wellbeing and keep you feeling full. That said, if you do eat avocado frequently, there are some things to keep in mind, Rizzo says, because it’s easy to go overboard without realizing. Is It Healthy to Eat Avocado Every Day? An avocado is a nutrient-dense whole plant food, and technically a fruit. Avocados are well known for being rich in heart-healthy monounsaturated fats, Rizzo says, but that’s far from where their benefits end. You’ll also find gut- and heart-healthy fiber in avocado, Rizzo explains, as well as potassium, folate, vitamin K, vitamin E and other vitamins, minerals and plant compounds. Plus, the combination of fiber and unsaturated fat “makes avocado very satiating,” she adds. So, are avocados healthy enough to eat every day? “Yes,” Rizzo says. “There’s no reason a healthy person can’t eat avocado every day if they enjoy it and it fits into their overall diet.” However, because avocados are so rich in fat, they are also surprisingly high in calories — higher than most fruits and vegetables, Rizzo notes. A standard serving is just one third of an avocado, which contains 80 calories, 3 grams of fiber, 7 grams of fat and 1 gram of protein. So, while avocado is a healthy, nutritious food that you can eat daily if you want, Rizzo says, “you don’t need to eat avocado every day to be healthy, and you can also get unsaturated fat from nuts, seeds and olive oil.” If You Want to Eat Avocado Daily... As healthy as avocados are, there are some points to keep in mind if you want to eat them every single day. Keep Portion Size in Mind Of course, there’s nothing wrong with eating a whole avocado once in a while. But if you want to eat avocado every single day, keep in mind that the normal serving size is just a third of a medium-sized avocado. Make It a More Complete Meal If you’re only eating a standard serving of avocado every day, it’s worth rounding out your meal with other complementary nutrients. “I like making (avocado toast) a more complete meal by using whole-grain bread and adding a protein source, like an egg, beans or hemp seeds,” Rizzo says. “Avocado is also great in grain bowls, bean salads, tacos and sandwiches, or mashed into a quick guacamole.” Get Other Sources of Healthy Fat If you like avocado enough to eat it every day, that’s great! But it pays to get a variety of healthy fat sources in your diet, Rizzo says. Consider mixing up your diet a little with nuts, seeds, nut butters, fatty fish and healthy cooking oils as well.

articles.title: Burgers Have Meat and Vegetables. Why Aren’t They Considered Healthy? A Dietitian Explains
articles.summary: The burger is meat and veggies, shouldn’t it be considered healthy? A dietitian explains why this protein-dense and vitamin-loaded meal is still an indulgence. Plus, how to tweak it.
articles.body: The burger is touted as a treat. It’s the greasy indulgence at the end of a long, fun night. Given, however, that the dish consists of ingredients hailed for their nutrients and protein content thanks to the meat and vegetables, you could argue that the meal should be considered healthy. So, what gives? A few things. Registered dietitian and author Erin Palinski-Wade would back this claim if it weren’t for select fixings and cooking techniques customary to making a burger. They’re responsible for rendering the burger calorically dense and less healthy than other meat and veggie dishes out there. If you are looking make the burger a part of your nutritious meal rotation, however, you can always tweak it. Make a play on the classic and create a better-for-you version of the burger, says Palinski-Wade. But there’s no reason you can’t stick to the classic recipe either. You could fit the burger into your balanced diet, reserving space for the dish in moderation. Whichever you choose, it’s worth familiarizing yourself with the burger’s nutritional content and why, despite some of its traditionally healthy components, it maintains its reputation. From there, you can decide how you’ll make it work for you and your health goals. Are Burgers Healthy or Not? “A burger itself isn’t inherently unhealthy. The portion, add-ons and sides can all contribute to the benefit (or negative impact) it can have on health,” Palinski-Wade tells TODAY.com. Take the beef. It offers protein, vitamins and other nutrients. Then you’ve got the lettuce and tomato with their vitamins and antioxidants. “Where calories can add up quickly is with a larger, higher-fat patty, added cheese, mayo or special sauce, cooking oil and an oversized bun,” says Palinski-Wade. “Layer those together, and you can end up with a meal that is much higher in calories, saturated fat, refined carbohydrates and sodium than you might expect.” How you cook the meat makes a difference too. The high temperatures required of grilling or searing a burger patty can produce compounds called heterocyclic amines, says Palinski-Wade. These chemicals can cause changes in DNA and increase your cancer risk, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Burger Nutrition The exact nutritional information for a burger will vary depending on how it’s cooked, its size and its toppings. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture database, you’ll find that each of a burger’s components typically has: Beef (100 Grams, 80% Lean Meat and 20% Fat) 243 calories17.5 grams protein19.4 grams fat0 grams carbohydrate0 grams fiber0 grams sugar Lettuce (1 Cup Shredded) 5 calories1 grams protein0 grams fat1 grams carbohydrates1 grams fiber0 grams sugar Tomato 22 calories0.7 grams protein0.42 grams fat3.84 grams carbohydrates1 gram fiber0 grams sugar Burger Bun 279 calories9.77 grams protein3.91 grams fat50.1 grams carbohydrates1.8 grams fiber7.28 grams sugar Ketchup (1 Tablespoon) 17.2 calories0.17 grams protein0.017 grams fat4.66 grams carbohydrates0.051 grams fiber3.62 grams sugar Mayonnaise (1 Tablespoon) 93.8 calories0.132 grams protein10.3 grams fat0.079 grams carbohydrates0 grams fiber0.079 grams sugar Cheese (1 Slice, Sharp Cheddar) 115 calories6.78 grams protein9.46 grams fat0.59 grams carbohydrates0 grams fiber0.076 grams sugar In a burger’s beef patty, you’ll also find approximately 2.5 milligrams of iron to carry oxygen throughout the body. You can count on 5.4 milligrams of zinc for immune function and 2.5 micrograms of vitamin B12 for healthy nerves and blood cells, Palinksi-Wade points out. The lettuce and tomato in a burger, on the other hand, offer up volume with few calories, plus a host of nutrients. From the lettuce, you’ll get a dose of vitamins A and K for immune and bone support respectively, adds Palinksi-Wade. And from the tomato, vitamin C, for antioxidants and iron absorption, among other benefits. There’s also potassium, vitamin A and the antioxidant lycopene for its antioxidant properties. The pillowy bun with its refined carbs and sugars, the condiments, the oils, cheese and the fries on the side, are what send the calories soaring and leave most of the burger’s nutrients overshadowed by high amounts of grease and sodium. How to Make a Healthier Burger Resist labeling a burger “good” or “bad,” Palinski-Wade recommends. Instead, work it into your healthy diet and eat burgers sparingly during the occasional outing or indulgent at-home dinner. If you want to rework the burger, Palinski-Wade offers her advice. Beef is already pretty nutrient-dense, she says. But if you’re looking to up the ante, opt for beef with an even lower fat content, such as one with 90% lean meat and 10% fat. “It provides all of the same beneficial nutrients with less saturated fat, making it a better choice for long term health,” she says. Less saturated fat means lower chances of increasing your LDL or “bad” cholesterol, which can increase your risk of heart disease and stroke. “Ground turkey breast, ground lean pork, ground lean chicken or bison can provide additional options if you want to vary your lean protein sources,” she adds. You might even blend mushrooms into your burger patties to lessen the amount of meat you use and lower your calorie intake, TODAY.com previously suggested. Next, consider portion size. Most restaurants are dishing up 6- to 8-ounce patties. “The larger the portion size, the higher the content of calories, fat, and refined carbohydrates, which can have a negative impact on health if consumed too often,” Palinski-Wade says. Instead, make your burgers at home and stick to 3- to 4-ounce servings. The most decadent burgers are dripping in sauces, from oils to condiments. And while that’s delicious every once in a while, opt for mustard, or a different light spread or dressing as an alternative to ketchup and mayo when making them at home. You might also consider leaving off the cheese and bacon and, instead, loading up on lettuce, tomato and onions for volume, fiber and fewer calories, says Palinksi-Wade. And sure, the best-in-class burgers are synonymous with french fries, but you don’t have to give up the sides completely. “Pairing your burger with a salad or fruit instead of fries can completely change the overall nutrient profile. You can also choose a whole-grain bun or lettuce wrap, depending on your preferences,” adds Palinski-Wade. “Rather than thinking of a burger as automatically unhealthy, I’d look at how it’s built,” she says.
